newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: CIS leaders vow to defend border with Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: CIS leaders vow to defend border with Afghanistan.

text.p: The leaders of five former Soviet states voiced concern on Friday at the rise to power in Afghanistan of a radical Islamic militia and said they would take steps to prevent fighting from spilling over the border.
A summit meeting in the Kazakh capital Almaty also denouced what the leaders described as atrocities committed by the Taleban militia after the seizure of the capital Kabul last week.
The meeting was attended by the presidents of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, as well as by Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.

Uzbek President Islam Karimov said Afghan warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who holds sway in northern regions, was the only buffer between the Taleban and the territory of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).

Karimov said that Dostum, who controls a strategic tunnel to northern Afghanistan, deserved stronger support from the neighbouring former Soviet states who are now part of the 12-member CIS, formed on the ashes of the Soviet Union.
"If this tunnel is surrendered, they (Taleban) will have no obstacle on their way northwards and we don't know how far they may go," Karimov told a joint news conference.
"If we do not want the (Afghan) war to escalate, if we want to force all parties to the negotiating table, we have to make sure that Dostum keeps the tunnel under his control," he said.

But there was no indication that the other CIS leaders shared his view. Kazakhstan's President Nursultan Nazarbayev made clear that the CIS would steer clear of involvement unless the conflict threatened the group's borders.
"We are strongly against interference in Afghanistan's internal affairs," Nazarbayev said.
Nazarbayev said that the five summit participants would take unspecified "adequate measures" if the fighting spilled over. But other participants made clear there would be no tough action until then.
"We call upon all sides to stop hostilities and restart peace talks," Nazarbayev said.
Nazarbayev said he, Chernomyrdin, Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov, Uzbekistan's Karimov and Kyrgyzstan President Askar Akayev wanted the U.N. Security Council to meet on Afghanistan.
He also said the five countries would start supplying northern Afghanistan with humanitarian aid to help the war-stricken civilian population.

"We denounce executions and violations of human rights committed lately in Afghanistan," he added, referring to the execution of some of the Taleban's political opponents in Kabul after the city's fall.
Chernomyrdin said he thought that the future stand of the CIS states would largely depend on further steps by other countries which have an impact on the situation in Afghanistan.
"We are watching attentively what other countries are doing, including the United States and Pakistan," he said. "This, of course, will influence our position."
Karimov said no extra troops from the CIS states would be sent to the areas bordering on Afghanistan. "There will be no reinforcements in the south," he said. "This is our common decision."
